stem: The phase of large-scale industrial production before the coming of factories is called:
solution: Proto-industrialisation was the phase of large-scale industrial production for the international market based not on factories but on decentralised, home-based work.

stem: In proto-industrialisation, merchants got goods produced by:
options: Peasants and artisans working in their own homes (the putting-out system)
solution: Merchants supplied money and raw materials to peasants/artisans who produced goods at home — the 'putting-out' system.

stem: The first symbol of the new industrial era in Britain was the:
solution: Cotton was the first symbol of the new industrial era; its production boomed in the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

stem: The inventor associated with the cotton spinning mill (the water frame) was:
solution: Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, bringing spinning processes together under one roof and management.

stem: The steam engine, which powered the Industrial Revolution, was improved by:
solution: James Watt improved the steam engine (patented 1781), making it a key power source for factories.

stem: The Spinning Jenny, a machine that speeded up spinning, was invented by:
solution: James Hargreaves invented the Spinning Jenny, which sped up the spinning process and reduced the demand for labour.

stem: Women workers in the woollen industry sometimes attacked the Spinning Jenny because they:
options: Feared it would take away their jobs
solution: Women who survived on hand spinning feared that the Spinning Jenny would take away their jobs, and some attacked the new machines.

stem: In 19th-century Britain, industrialists were often slow to introduce machines because:
options: There was plenty of cheap human labour available
solution: With a large supply of cheap labour, industrialists often preferred hand labour to expensive machines, so machines spread slowly in many sectors.

stem: Before European companies gained power, India was a leading exporter of:
solution: India was a major exporter of fine cotton and silk textiles in the world market before industrial Britain overtook it.

stem: The important Indian textile ports whose trade declined under Company rule included Surat and:
solution: The old ports of Surat and Hooghly declined as European companies shifted trade to the new colonial ports of Bombay and Calcutta.

stem: The paid servant appointed by the East India Company to supervise weavers and collect cloth was the:
solution: The gomastha was the paid servant/agent appointed by the Company to supervise weavers, collect supplies and check cloth quality.

stem: Indian weavers suffered under the Company because they:
options: Lost bargaining power, received low prices and fell into debt through advances
solution: Tied to the Company through advances (loans) and controlled by gomasthas, weavers lost bargaining power, got low prices and often fell into debt.

stem: Indian handloom weavers were ruined in the 19th century mainly by:
options: The flood of cheap machine-made cloth from Manchester
solution: Cheap machine-made cloth imported from Manchester (Britain) undercut Indian handloom cloth, ruining the weavers.

stem: The first cotton mill in India was set up in 1854 in:
solution: India's first cotton mill was established in Bombay in 1854.

stem: The first jute mills in India were set up in which region?
solution: The first jute mills were set up in Bengal, close to the jute-growing areas.

stem: The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) was set up in 1907 at:
solution: TISCO was established at Jamshedpur in 1907 by Jamsetji Tata, becoming a landmark of Indian industrialisation.

stem: The early Indian industrialists who set up factories included:
solution: Early Indian industrialists like Dwarkanath Tagore, Jamsetji Tata and Seth Hukumchand set up mills and factories.

stem: The Swadeshi Movement helped Indian industry by:
options: Encouraging the use of Indian goods and boycott of foreign cloth
solution: The Swadeshi Movement encouraged Indians to buy Indian-made goods and boycott foreign cloth, boosting Indian industry.

stem: During the First World War, Indian industries grew because:
options: British imports declined and Indian mills supplied war needs
solution: During WWI, British mills were busy with war production, so imports to India fell and Indian mills expanded to meet local and war demand.

stem: Despite factories, a large part of India's industrial production continued to come from:
solution: Even in the age of factories, much of India's industrial production continued to come from small-scale and handloom/handicraft producers.

stem: Manufacturers used __________ to create a market for their goods.
solution: Manufacturers used advertisements, attractive labels and images to expand the market and sell their goods.

stem: Manchester manufacturers put labels with images of __________ on cloth to appeal to Indian buyers.
solution: To appeal to Indian buyers, Manchester manufacturers printed labels with images of Indian gods and goddesses on their cloth.

stem: Industrialisation in Britain first developed most strongly in which two sectors?
solution: The Industrial Revolution developed first and most strongly in the cotton and metal (iron) industries in Britain.

stem: Life for workers in early industrial Britain was often marked by:
options: Low wages, unemployment and harsh living/working conditions
solution: Early industrial workers faced low wages, seasonal unemployment, and harsh, unhealthy living and working conditions.

stem: The fear of unemployment made many workers:
options: Hostile to the introduction of new machines
solution: Because machines threatened jobs, many workers were hostile to their introduction, fearing unemployment.

stem: The decline of Indian textile exports under colonial rule is an example of:
solution: The ruin of India's textile industry and its craft producers under colonialism is an example of de-industrialisation.

stem: The gomastha system led to conflicts because gomasthas:
options: Acted arrogantly, punished weavers and controlled them
solution: Gomasthas were often outsiders who acted arrogantly, punished weavers for delays and tightly controlled them, causing conflicts.

stem: The industrial market in India was dominated by British goods until Indian industry grew, especially in:
solution: British cotton textiles dominated the Indian market until Indian cotton mills grew, especially from the late 19th century onwards.

stem: One reason Indian entrepreneurs initially focused on export markets (like China) was that:
options: The home market was dominated by British imports
solution: Since the Indian home market was dominated by British imports, early Indian industrialists often exported (e.g. yarn to China) before the home market opened up.

stem: The 'putting-out' system linked town merchants with:
options: Village producers who worked at home
solution: The putting-out system linked town merchants who supplied raw materials with village producers who made goods in their homes.

stem: The pace of industrial change in Britain in the 19th century is best described as:
solution: Industrial change was gradual and uneven; traditional industries and hand labour continued alongside the new factories.

stem: The demand for hand-made goods with fine designs continued because:
options: Machines could not make certain intricate or specialised products
There was no demand for machine goods
solution: Machines could not produce certain intricate designs and specialised goods, so there remained a demand for skilled hand-made products.

stem: The growth of Indian-owned industries was aided by nationalist sentiment because:
options: Swadeshi encouraged Indians to buy Indian goods
solution: Nationalist (Swadeshi) sentiment encouraged Indians to buy Indian-made goods, helping the growth of Indian-owned industries.

stem: The seasonal nature of demand in many industries meant that:
options: Industrialists preferred hand labour they could hire and fire as needed
solution: Where demand was seasonal, industrialists preferred flexible hand labour they could hire and dismiss as needed, rather than costly machines.

stem: The decline of the old ports (Surat, Hooghly) and rise of new ones (Bombay, Calcutta) reflected the:
options: Shift of trade control to European companies
solution: The decline of Surat/Hooghly and rise of Bombay/Calcutta reflected how European companies redirected and controlled trade.

stem: The overall effect of British industrialisation on Indian crafts was:
options: Decline and ruin of many traditional crafts and weavers
solution: British industrialisation and cheap imports led to the decline and ruin of many Indian traditional crafts and weavers.

stem: Which of the following pairs (person — contribution) is correctly matched?
solution: Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill. James Watt improved the steam engine, James Hargreaves the Spinning Jenny, and Jamsetji Tata founded TISCO.

stem: The workers who lost jobs to machines sometimes responded by:
solution: Some workers who lost jobs to machines responded by attacking or breaking them, fearing unemployment.

stem: The Indian cotton mill industry grew fastest in cities like:
solution: The cotton mill industry in India grew fastest in Bombay and Ahmedabad, which had access to raw cotton, ports and capital.

stem: The relationship between the Company and Indian weavers was characterised by:
options: Control through advances, gomasthas and low prices
solution: The Company controlled weavers through advances (loans), gomasthas and by fixing low prices, tying them to its supply system.

stem: One reason British goods could undersell Indian handmade goods was:
solution: Machine (factory) production made British goods cheaper, allowing them to undersell Indian handmade goods.

stem: The industrialisation of Britain and the de-industrialisation of India were linked because:
options: India became a market for British goods and a supplier of raw materials
solution: Britain industrialised partly by using India as a market for its manufactured goods and a supplier of cheap raw materials, deindustrialising India.

stem: The survival of small-scale and handloom production shows that industrialisation:
options: Did not completely wipe out traditional production
solution: The survival of handloom and small-scale production shows that industrialisation did not entirely replace traditional forms of production.

stem: Advertising was important in the age of industrialisation because it:
options: Created demand and shaped consumer tastes for new products
solution: Advertising helped create demand and shape consumer tastes, expanding the market for industrial products.

stem: Indian jute mills competed with which foreign producers?
solution: Indian jute mills in Bengal competed with the jute mills of Dundee (Scotland) in the global market.

stem: The colonial government's policy generally favoured:
options: British manufactured goods over Indian industry
solution: Colonial policy generally favoured British manufactured goods, often at the expense of Indian industry and crafts.

stem: The market for industrial goods expanded as manufacturers:
options: Sought new consumers through advertising, labels and new products
solution: Manufacturers expanded markets by seeking new consumers, using advertising, attractive labels and by introducing new products.

stem: The industrialisation process created a new class of:
solution: Industrialisation created new social classes — industrial workers (the proletariat) and factory owners/capitalists.

stem: The Indian textile industry recovered and grew in the 20th century partly due to:
options: Swadeshi, WWI demand, and Indian entrepreneurship
solution: Indian textiles recovered due to the Swadeshi movement, increased demand during WWI, and the growth of Indian-owned mills and entrepreneurship.

stem: The cotton spinning mill and the water frame are associated with the inventor:
solution: Richard Arkwright created the cotton mill, bringing the costly new machines under one roof, and is associated with the water frame, marking a shift to factory production.

stem: The Spinning Jenny, which speeded up the spinning process, was invented by:
solution: James Hargreaves devised the Spinning Jenny in 1764, a machine that allowed one worker to spin several threads at once, boosting spinning output.

stem: The steam engine that powered the Industrial Revolution was greatly improved by:
solution: James Watt improved the earlier Newcomen steam engine and, with the manufacturer Matthew Boulton, produced the new steam engine that powered factories.

stem: James Watt's steam engine was manufactured and marketed with the support of the industrialist:
solution: Matthew Boulton, a manufacturer, financed and marketed James Watt's improved steam engine, which was patented in 1781.

stem: The most dynamic industries in Britain during early industrialisation were cotton and:
solution: Cotton and metals were the most dynamic industries in Britain; cotton led the first phase of industrialisation up to the 1840s, after which the iron and steel industry led the way.

stem: The first cotton mill in India was set up in 1854 in the city of:
solution: The first cotton mill in India was established in Bombay in 1854, and it began production two years later.

stem: The Elgin Mill, an early industrial enterprise, was set up in the city of:
solution: In Kanpur, the Elgin Mill was started in the 1860s, and the first cotton mill of Ahmedabad and others followed, expanding factory industry beyond Bombay and Bengal.

stem: The paid servant appointed by the East India Company to supervise weavers, collect goods and examine cloth quality was the:
solution: The Company appointed a paid servant called the gomastha to supervise weavers, collect supplies, and examine the quality of cloth, bypassing the traditional traders and brokers.

stem: The person who recruited and controlled new factory workers in Indian industry, an old and trusted employee of the industrialist, was the:
solution: Industrialists usually employed a 'jobber' to get new workers; he recruited people from his village, helped them settle, and often demanded money and favours in return, gaining much power.

stem: Before European companies gained power, India was the world's largest exporter of:
solution: Before the age of machine industries, silk and cotton goods from India dominated the international market in textiles; India was the world's leading exporter of cotton textiles.

stem: The Indian port through which much of the textile trade with West Asia flowed, and which declined as Company power grew, was:
solution: Old ports like Surat and Hooghly, through which Indian merchants had traded, declined as European companies gained power, while new colonial ports like Bombay and Calcutta grew.

stem: A fine cotton cloth exported from India that gave its name to a European term for muslin was:
solution: When European traders first saw fine cotton from Mosul (Iraq), they called all such cloth 'muslin'; a variety of Indian textiles like chintz, calico and bandanna also entered European languages.

stem: The word 'chintz', a printed cotton cloth, comes from the Hindi word:
solution: The word 'chintz' comes from the Hindi word 'chhint', a cloth with small and colourful flowery designs, showing India's influence on the global textile vocabulary.

stem: Workers in Britain who attacked and destroyed machines out of fear of unemployment were known as:
solution: Workers displaced by machines sometimes attacked them; the movement led by (the possibly mythical) Ned Ludd gave rise to the term 'Luddites' for machine-breakers.

stem: In the woollen industry, when the Spinning Jenny was introduced, it was attacked by:
options: Women who survived on hand spinning
solution: Women who survived on hand spinning feared that the Spinning Jenny would displace their labour and destroy their livelihoods, and so they attacked the new machines.

stem: The phase of large-scale industrial production for an international market not based on factories was called:
solution: Even before factories, there was large-scale industrial production for an international market, based on decentralised handwork in the countryside — this is called proto-industrialisation.

stem: In the proto-industrial system, town merchants got goods produced by:
options: Peasants and artisans in the countryside
solution: In proto-industrialisation, merchants from towns supplied money to peasants and artisans in the countryside to produce goods for the international market, within a 'putting-out' system.

stem: Manchester manufacturers pasted labels on cloth bundles going to India; the label 'MADE IN MANCHESTER' with images of Indian gods was meant to:
options: Make the cloth familiar and appealing to Indian buyers
solution: Manufacturers put labels with images of Indian gods and goddesses on their cloth to make the foreign product seem familiar and respectable to Indian buyers, using them as a marketing device.

stem: During the First World War, Indian industries grew mainly because:
options: British imports declined and factories supplied war needs
solution: During the First World War, British mills were busy with war production and stopped exporting to India; Indian factories got a vast home market and also supplied war needs (jute bags, cloth, boots), boosting industrial output.

stem: Despite the growth of factories, a large part of India's industrial output continued to come from the:
solution: Even in the 20th century, factory industries formed only a small part of the economy; much of India's industrial production continued to come from handloom weavers and small-scale producers, who adapted and survived.

stem: The handloom weavers survived partly because they:
options: Produced fine designs and specialised cloth that machines could not easily copy
solution: Handloom weavers survived by producing specialised and finely designed cloth (like the woven border sari) that could not be reproduced by machines and by adopting some new technology like the fly shuttle.

stem: The device adopted by Indian handloom weavers in the 20th century to increase productivity was the:
solution: By adopting the fly shuttle, weavers could increase their productivity and compete better, one reason handloom cloth production actually expanded in the 20th century.

stem: Indian handloom weavers were badly hurt in the 19th century mainly because:
options: Cheap machine-made British cloth flooded the Indian market
There was no demand for cloth
solution: Cheap machine-made cloth imported from Britain undersold Indian handmade cloth, and export markets collapsed, ruining large numbers of Indian weavers.

stem: Gomasthas often came into conflict with weavers because they:
options: Behaved arrogantly, punished weavers for delays and paid low prices
solution: Gomasthas were outsiders with no long-term social link to the villages; they acted arrogantly, marched into villages with sepoys and peons, and punished weavers for delays, breeding conflict.

stem: Under the Company's system, weavers lost their bargaining power because they were:
options: Given advances (loans) that tied them to the Company and could not sell to other buyers
solution: Weavers who took advances from the Company were bound to hand over the cloth they produced and could not take it to any other buyer, so they lost the freedom to bargain and sell in the open market.

stem: The early Indian industrialists and merchants who accumulated wealth through the China trade and then set up industries included:
solution: Merchants like Dwarkanath Tagore in Bengal and Parsi businessmen such as Dinshaw Petit and Jamsetjee Nusserwanjee Tata in Bombay made fortunes partly through the China trade and invested in industry.

stem: Assertion (A): Indian textile exports declined sharply in the 19th century. Reason (R): Cheap British machine-made cloth captured both the Indian and world markets.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: As industrial Britain flooded markets with cheap machine-made cloth, Indian handmade textiles could not compete, and Indian exports collapsed — R explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): British industrialists were sometimes slow to adopt new machines. Reason (R): There was plenty of cheap hand labour available, so machines were not always cost-effective.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Because human labour was cheap and abundant, many British industrialists preferred hand labour to costly machines, especially for goods with fluctuating or seasonal demand — R explains A.

stem: Match the person with the contribution: (i) Richard Arkwright (ii) James Watt (iii) James Hargreaves — (a) Steam engine (b) Spinning Jenny (c) Cotton mill:
solution: Arkwright is linked with the cotton mill, Watt with the improved steam engine, and Hargreaves with the Spinning Jenny.

stem: In early industrial Britain, workers faced great hardship, especially the abundance of job-seekers, which meant:
options: Low wages, seasonal unemployment and poor living conditions
solution: The abundance of labour meant low wages, and many workers faced seasonal unemployment, long waits for jobs, and miserable, overcrowded living conditions in industrial towns.

stem: The seasonal demand of many industries (like gas works and breweries) meant employers preferred:
options: Hand labour, hiring workers only for the season
solution: In industries with seasonal demand, employers preferred hand labour, hiring workers for the busy season, because installing expensive machines to run only part of the year was not worthwhile.

stem: The colonial government's economic policies in India generally favoured:
options: British manufactured imports over Indian industry
solution: Colonial policy, including tariff and trade rules, generally favoured British manufactured goods and hindered the growth of Indian industry, contributing to deindustrialisation.

stem: Indian jute mills in Bengal competed mainly with the jute producers of:
solution: The jute mills of Bengal competed with jute manufacturers of Dundee in Scotland, though Indian mills eventually gained an advantage due to proximity to raw jute.

stem: The first phase of the Industrial Revolution in Britain was led by the cotton industry, which relied on raw cotton imported largely from:
solution: The rapidly growing British cotton industry depended on raw cotton imports, chiefly from colonies and plantations in India and the American South.

stem: The Indian cotton mill industry was concentrated most heavily in the cities of:
solution: The cotton mill industry in India grew fastest in western India, especially in Bombay and Ahmedabad, close to the cotton-growing regions.

stem: The pace of industrial change in nineteenth-century Britain is best described as:
options: Gradual, with old and new sectors coexisting
solution: Industrialisation was gradual: the most dynamic sectors (cotton, metals) grew fast, but traditional industries and hand technologies continued alongside them well into the 19th century.

stem: The Manchester goods that flooded India during the 19th century were mainly:
solution: Manchester in England became the centre of cotton manufacture, and its cheap machine-made cotton cloth was exported in huge quantities to India, undercutting local weavers.

stem: The decline of Indian handicrafts under colonial rule is an example of:
solution: The ruin of traditional Indian crafts and the collapse of textile exports under colonial policies is described as deindustrialisation — the reverse of what happened in Britain.

stem: The steam engine and factory system in Britain marked a shift from human/animal power to:
solution: The steam engine, using coal, provided a new and powerful source of mechanical energy that freed industry from dependence on water power and animal muscle, driving factory production.

stem: The industrial workers in Britain, faced with fear of unemployment from machines, sometimes:
options: Opposed and destroyed machines (as the Luddites did)
solution: Fearing that machines would take away their jobs, some workers resisted mechanisation, and machine-breaking (Luddism) became one form of protest in early industrial Britain.

stem: The survival of handloom and small-scale production alongside factories shows that industrialisation:
options: Did not immediately or completely replace older forms of production
solution: Even after the rise of factories, handmade production persisted and even grew in some sectors, showing that industrialisation was uneven and did not wipe out older forms of production.

stem: The first Indian jute mill was set up in 1855 at Rishra, near Calcutta, by the Bengali entrepreneur/company because Bengal was the region that grew:
solution: Jute mills were set up in Bengal because it was close to the raw-jute growing areas; the first mill came up at Rishra in 1855.

stem: The Tata Iron and Steel Company benefited during the First World War because:
options: The colonial government needed steel for railways and war supplies
solution: During the First World War, imports of British steel to India declined and the colonial government needed steel for rails and munitions, so TISCO got large orders and expanded rapidly.

stem: The market for goods was expanded by manufacturers through advertising and by:
options: Making new consumer needs appear natural and desirable
solution: Manufacturers used advertisements and appealing images to persuade people that they needed new products, thereby creating new consumers and expanding the market for industrial goods.

stem: Industrialisation created a new social class of factory owners (industrialists) and a class of:
solution: Industrialisation gave rise to a new class of industrialists and a large working class of factory labourers, transforming the social structure of industrial societies.

stem: The overall theme of 'The Age of Industrialisation' is how:
options: Industrialisation transformed production and society, with different effects in Britain and colonial India
solution: The chapter explains how industrialisation transformed production and society, contrasting Britain's factory growth with the de-industrialisation and later revival of industry in colonial India.
